js_003: Who wrote A Journey to Mujin?
js_008: A Journey to Mujin is a short story Kim Seung-ok published in 1964. With his sensory style, he opened new ground for modern Korean fiction.
js_010: Which best describes this work’s genre?
js_014: A lyric poem written in meter
js_015: A Journey to Mujin is a short story. Published in the magazine Sasanggye in 1964, it’s a short but deeply resonant masterpiece by Kim Seung-ok.
js_017: In which magazine did the novel first appear in 1964?
js_022: A Journey to Mujin appeared in Sasanggye in October 1964. It stirred a strong response from the moment it was published.
js_024: What’s the name of the first-person protagonist who leads the novel?
js_029: The protagonist and narrator is Yun Hui-jung, a man around thirty who quietly recounts his few days in Mujin through his own eyes.
js_031: The hometown the protagonist visits, a town famous for its fog, is?
js_036: The protagonist’s hometown is Mujin, a city of fog. It’s a fictional place that doesn’t really exist, modeled on the author’s hometown of Suncheon.
js_038: What does the novel name as Mujin’s local specialty?
js_043: Mujin has no real specialty; if anything, it’s the fog. That thick fog is the core symbol wrapping the whole novel.
js_045: Which is the right reason the protagonist went down to Mujin?
js_046: To rest a while at his wife’s urging, before a promotion
js_047: To flee to his beloved hometown after his business collapsed
js_048: To be at his aging mother’s deathbed
js_049: To hold a wedding with an old lover
js_050: On the verge of a promotion to director, the protagonist goes down to Mujin for a short rest at his wife’s urging — a brief escape before climbing the ladder.
js_052: What kind of company does the protagonist work at in Seoul?
js_057: The protagonist works at a pharmaceutical company in Seoul — one owned by his wife’s family, where he’s about to become an executive.
js_059: What position is the protagonist set to rise to after his trip to Mujin?
js_064: The protagonist is set to be promoted to managing director of his in-laws’ company. That climb is what calls him back from Mujin to reality.
js_066: The name of the music teacher the protagonist meets at a drinking party in Mujin and is drawn to?
js_071: The woman the protagonist is drawn to is Ha In-suk, a music teacher at Mujin Middle School. She longs desperately to leave Mujin for Seoul.
js_078: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture “A Journey to Mujin”
js_079: Digital Suncheon Culture Encyclopedia “Kim Seung-ok’s Journey to Mujin”
js_080: Kim Seung-ok (1941– ) debuted in 1962 and, with his sensory style, portrayed the urbanization and human alienation of the 1960s. A Journey to Mujin and Seoul, Winter 1964 are his signature works.
js_081: A Journey to Mujin is a short piece, yet through a few days in a fog-bound city it renders in depth the inner life of a man wavering between the ideal and reality.
js_082: A Journey to Mujin appeared in the magazine Sasanggye in October 1964. Ever since, it has been counted among the peaks of the modern Korean short story.
js_083: The narrator, Yun Hui-jung, is a man around thirty. Through his first-person eyes, a few hazy, fog-like days in Mujin unfold quietly.
js_084: Mujin is a fictional city that doesn’t really exist. Modeled on the author’s hometown of Suncheon in South Jeolla, it was created as a fog-covered symbolic space.
js_085: Mujin has no notable specialty; if anything, it’s the fog. That thick fog wraps the whole work, creating an atmosphere of reverie and escape.
js_086: On the verge of a promotion to director, the protagonist goes down to Mujin for a short rest at his wife’s urging. That brief escape before success becomes the story’s starting point.
js_087: The protagonist works at a pharmaceutical company owned by his wife’s family. This position, gained through marriage, is the tie that binds him back to reality.
js_088: The protagonist is set to become managing director of his in-laws’ company. His escapade in Mujin ends, in the end, before this rise to success.
js_089: Ha In-suk is a music teacher at Mujin Middle School. Toward her, longing to get out to Seoul, the protagonist feels both pity and attraction.
js_103: Mujin’s only specialty. Enveloping the whole city and blurring reality, it’s the work’s core image, symbolizing reverie, loss of self, and escape.
js_105: A fictional city whose name means ‘fog ferry.’ Modeled on the author’s hometown of Suncheon, it’s a symbolic space where ideal, unconscious, and escape entangle.
js_106: The first-person narrator and protagonist. A man around thirty on the verge of success, he wavers between the ideal (Mujin) and reality (Seoul).
js_107: A music teacher who majored in vocal music at a Seoul conservatory. Longing to leave Mujin for Seoul, she sings the popular song Tears of Mokpo at a drinking party.
js_109: The protagonist’s middle-school classmate and Mujin’s tax-office chief. He’s drawn as the face of snobbish worldliness — the local boy who made good.
js_111: A guileless junior teacher of Korean at his old school. Secretly in love with Ha In-suk, he’s an untainted figure set against Cho.
js_113: The wife’s telegram calling him to Seoul is reality’s summons; the letter he writes to Ha In-suk and then tears up is a folded-away sincerity. Two slips of paper decide the ending.
js_115: The achievement of Kim Seung-ok’s writing, portraying 1960s urbanization and human alienation in a sensory style. It’s called the expression that changed the course of modern Korean fiction.
js_118: Leaving Seoul, the protagonist heads for fog-wrapped Mujin.
js_119: It’s a trip he takes at his wife’s urging, before a promotion to director.
js_120: The closer the bus gets to Mujin, the thicker the fog settles.
js_121: Boredom on the edge of success and a hazy heart flow together.
js_123: A drinking party opens at the home of Cho, a classmate turned tax-office chief.
js_124: The music teacher Ha In-suk sings the popular song Tears of Mokpo.
js_125: Mr. Park, a guileless junior who loves Ha In-suk, is there too.
js_126: The protagonist feels pity for Ha In-suk, who longs to go to Seoul.
js_128: The long seawall reaching to the sea
js_129: The protagonist and Ha In-suk walk together along the seawall to the sea.
js_130: On the seawall they come upon the corpse of a bar woman who took her own life.
js_131: The two spend a night together and grow closer.
js_132: A promise to take her to Seoul passes between them.
js_135: A telegram from his wife arrives, urging him to hurry back to Seoul.
js_136: He tears up the letter he wrote to Ha In-suk, never sending it.
js_137: The protagonist leaves Mujin and returns to the reality of Seoul.
js_138: Looking at the signpost, he feels a deep shame.
js_140: A Journey to Mujin, and after
js_141: It becomes the peak of the sensory style called a revolution of sensibility.
js_142: In 1967 it was also made into the film Mist, with a screenplay by Kim Seung-ok.
js_143: It’s loved enough that the Kim Seung-ok Literary Award was established in his honor.
js_144: The question of shame between reality and the ideal still holds today.
js_145: The night she sang Tears of Mokpo
js_146: Ha In-suk, who majored in vocal music at a Seoul conservatory, can’t refuse the tax chief’s request and sings the popular song Tears of Mokpo at the party. It’s a night when talent loses its place.
js_147: It makes you think about what a person gives up when the talent they hold loses its place to stand.
js_149: On the seawall to the sea, the protagonist passes indifferently by the corpse of a bar woman who killed herself. It’s a scene where the death and emptiness hanging over the foggy city surface, chill and clear.
js_150: It asks again what a heart, gone numb before another’s death, has actually lost.
js_152: The protagonist tears up, himself, the letter he wrote to Ha In-suk promising to take her to Seoul — never sending it. It’s a moment of self-deception, folding away sincerity before reality.
js_153: It makes you think about the promises we fail to keep and the shame they leave behind.
js_154: Why might we need a hazy, fog-like time of escape?
js_155: Think about both what the days in Mujin gave the protagonist and what they took away.
js_156: Like Ha In-suk, whose talent lost its place, what do we give up as we live?
js_157: Weigh the sorrow in the scene where she, a vocal-music major, sings a popular tune.
js_158: When he makes a promise he can’t keep and tears up the letter, where does Yun Hui-jung’s shame come from?
js_159: Read it as shame that comes from honestly facing the self that chose reality.
